p.x:
There are five people in my family, and we are all very different. My father is a serious man. He works hard and he is always honest. My mother is calm and patient; she never shouts. My older brother is brave. Last year, he saved a dog from the river!
My little sister is very talkative and cheerful. She talks all day, from breakfast to bedtime. Sometimes she is a bit bossy with her friends. And me? I'm quite shy. I don't like speaking in front of the class, but I'm friendly when you know me.
Our cat, Mali, is the laziest member of the family. She sleeps for eighteen hours a day! My grandmother says it's rude to put the cat on the table, but we sometimes do it anyway.

p.t: Are You an Introvert or an Extrovert?
p.x:
Psychologists often describe people as introverts or extroverts. Extroverts are outgoing and sociable. They enjoy parties, meeting new people and being the centre of attention. They often feel bored when they are alone.
Introverts, on the other hand, prefer quiet activities and small groups. This doesn't mean they are shy or unfriendly. Many introverts are good listeners and very thoughtful. They simply need time alone to recharge their energy after social events.
Most people are a mix of both. You might be easy-going with friends but cautious with strangers. Your mood can also change: everyone is a little moody sometimes!
Some personality types can cause problems at work. Stubborn people find it hard to accept other ideas, and arrogant people may not listen to their colleagues. Sensitive people may be hurt by criticism. On the other hand, modest workers often don't get credit for their success. Optimistic people tend to cope better with stress than pessimistic ones, while curious people often learn faster. Selfish or careless behaviour, however, is a problem in any team.

For decades, psychologists believed that personality was fixed by early adulthood. Our basic temperament, they argued, was largely inherited, and traits such as being impulsive or conscientious would remain stable throughout life.
More recent research challenges this view. Long-term studies tracking thousands of people have found that personality continues to develop well into old age. On average, people become more conscientious, more emotionally stable and more agreeable as they grow older, a pattern some researchers call 'the maturity principle'. Life events also play a role: starting a demanding job may make someone more meticulous, while a serious illness may make them more empathetic.
Can we change deliberately? Some experiments suggest we can, at least to a degree. Participants who set specific goals, such as becoming more assertive by expressing their opinions in meetings, showed measurable changes after several months. However, change requires consistent effort, and personality rarely transforms completely.
Interestingly, the traits society admires are not always the most useful. Charismatic leaders attract followers, but research suggests that humble leaders often build stronger teams. Similarly, a tactful manager who delivers criticism kindly may achieve more than one who is brilliant but harsh. And while trusting others is generally positive, being too gullible can leave people open to manipulation. Personality, it seems, is less about having the 'right' traits than about knowing when to use them.
